Five ways of defining exploratory testing. 
1) Session-based (solve management)
2) Manual (tester work, pick what interests us)
3) Technique (fits old views of testing without adaptations)
4) 3.0 (protects from "checking")
5) Contemporary (values kindness and automation)

object.content:
The what is what in world of (open-source) software is hard one. The whole concept of being able to repackage whatever someone created to a new name makes it hard to track what is what. We have this "superb-test-framework" with internal code name, and turns out is a way of saying someone added a few lines of code on top of another framework.

Concepts like #playwright being #library on python and #framework on javascript are very difficult for people who think one name means one thing.

Create a talk description for a talk on errors of omission

Errors of omission are a common and often overlooked problem in software development. They occur when important information is left out or ignored, and can have serious consequences for the quality and reliability of the software. In this talk, we will explore the concept of errors of omission and discuss strategies for identifying and mitigating these errors in the software development process. We will also discuss real-world examples of errors of omission and their impact on software projects. By the end of this talk, attendees will have a better understanding of the importance of addressing errors of omission, and will have gained practical knowledge and techniques for identifying and preventing these errors in their own software development efforts.

attachment.name:
Generated response. 

How to test login? To test a login feature, you can follow these steps:

1. Verify that the login form is displayed on the page and is in the correct location.

2. Enter valid login credentials and verify that the user is able to log in successfully.

3. Enter invalid login credentials, such as an incorrect password, and verify that the user is not able to log in and that an error message is displayed.

4. Try logging in using different input methods, such as typing, copying and pasting, or using a virtual keyboard, and verify that the login form works correctly with all input methods.

5. Test the login feature in different browsers and on different devices to ensure that it works consistently across different environments.

6. If the login feature has any additional features, such as a "remember me" option or a password reset function, test those features to ensure they are working correctly.

7. If the login feature is part of a larger system, test the login feature in the context of the system to ensure that it works correctly and integrates properly with other components.

8. If the login feature has any security measures, such as CAPTCHA or two-factor authentication, test those measures to ensure they are working properly.

9. If the login feature is part of a larger form, test the form as a whole to ensure that the login feature works properly in the context of the form.

object.content: How to get to joy of discovery when working under continuous rush and stress? This was asked at #ATAGTR2022. I don't work under continuous rush and stress because I frame what I do differently. I have control over my calendar (the calendar does not have control over me). Continuous delivery without fixed release schedule allows to do all work needed before release, and release does not stop me from testing for things while in production. It is not my work, but our work.

object.content:
Today I am discovering the core lessons from my talk by listening to myself speak.

1. Prefer empty paper with a frame. It encourages integrating diverse perspectives in ways reviewing someone else's result never will.

2. Testing is applied steganography. Bugs are invisible ink of conversations we should be having.

3. Everything that does not need to be automated gets done while automating. This is subject to how you organize for testing. Do more of it on unit testing level.

#ATAGTR2022

There was a question about the company level description of "defect management process" and my first response is just a deep sigh.

As in yes we have routes in for different kinds of feedback. We seek some actively, and some we react to if it finds the right channels. That too is a journey, not a destination.

Basic Illusions: Code Making a Product

Code doing what it’s supposed to.
Product doing what it would need to.

Process being able to deliver with a change in mind

object.content: People say a lot that if you can't measure it, you can't improve it. Earlier tonight I was explaining, with a lot of certainty, that collecting stories (while it is sampling) isn't really measuring, but it helps you better than measuring to see if you have numbers of stories, recent stories or if you are stuck in repeating your old life accomplishments. Recounting stories, categorising those and seeing patterns in those isn't *measuring* as such, but most definitely help me more than numbers.

People keep saying that manual testing is time-consuming and error-prone, especially in comparisons with automated testing. With the amount of time we use on automated testing and the special profile of errors we catch and completely miss, it just isn't the dimension we should be discussing.

I use attended and unattended testing in frame of #ContemporaryExploratoryTesting. Results, direct costs and opportunities costs must be balanced, and we want systems do (some of) the work when we're gone.

Not all testers are worthless, some are net negative by holding on to work that should be shared with the team.

object.content:
The capabilities *intended* for this research are:
1) natural language processing to communicate successfully in a human language
2) knowledge representation to store what it knows or hears
3) automated reasoning to answer questions and to draw new conclusions
4) machine learning to adapt to new circumstances and to detect and extrapolate patterns.
5) computer vision and speech recognition to perceive the world
6) robotics to manipulate objects and move about.

object.content: There's an interesting balance of correctness and usefulness, one that is particularly visible in conversations of the new ML language model tools. There's a lot of conversation on how it is incorrect in relevant ways of wrong answers or reinforcing bias, but very little on how it is useful for many things we do now. Incorrect becomes more of a problem when people no longer recognise correctness and rely on the tools. Is it possible to have tools we don't fully rely on?

object.content: Test system that don’t rely on deterministic results. We build a lot of systems that repeat the same. But what if we actively vary paths by using model-based testing, vary data by randomized production sampling and generation. When our oracles can’t be more than partial looking for a specific pattern. When failing requires more analysis effort. Now that we built the deterministic one, it’s time to see this side further.

attachment.name:
from approvaltests import verify, verify_as_json

def test_branding(branding_resp):
    assert branding_resp.status_code == 200
    #Verify the entire json with approvaltests
    verify_as_json(branding_resp.json())
    #Search for some strong in the response text
    assert "Shady Meadows" in branding_resp.text
    #Search for specific value in specific place of json-structure
    assert branding_resp.json()["name"] == "Shady Meadows B&B"
    #Search deeper in structure and multiple items
    assert branding_resp.json()["map"]["latitude"] == 52.6351204 and branding_resp.json()["map"]["longitude"] == 1.2733774
    #Verify that there is a json structure present without caring about what is in it
    assert branding_resp.json()["description"]

object.content:
"How do you test localisations", I asked. Received a test case. Mentioned I knew that, but I did not know why they go through the moves they do. Turns out neither did they.

Drilled down into risks:
- some (new) strings may not be localizable
- the original and the localised file may have differences in contents and a missing string may cause problems
- there may be missing translated texts
- the translated texts may be mistranslated
...

If you rely on "test case", document why not just how.

attachment.name:
Sketchnote about what rebels what from their boss, by Tanmay Vora, collecting insights from rebelsatwork.com. 

1. We are not troublemakers, we are motivated make our org better
2. We care about work more than anyone else, that's why we are willing to engage in conflict
3. We need an environment where it is safe to disagree and challenge status quo
4. Love our differences and quicks, we may not be like you and that's a good thing
5. Challenge us, give us thorniest problems, let us prove our wild ideas at work, we want to be stretched
6. Don't give us lip service, tell us like it is. 
7. Coach us on how to navigate org. politics so we avoid making mistakes
8. Rebelliousness is a positive behaviour, its an act of courage and risk-taking
9. Appreciate us and we'll move mountains for you.

I keep sharing about this for people to understand that travel, even paying travel ahead of time, is a major blocker seeing a variety of faces in our conferences. Money (or time) is not equally available to all.

I'm not a developer advocate. My company lets me speak but does not ask me to speak. Speaking is my own time. This is what it has always been for me. For 511 sessions.

A year ago someone who had taken a 20 days retraining program to testing reached out to me. They were struggling at work. Only tester, no one to guide on expectations. I guided for an hour. Now I received a message thank you message telling they are excelling at work, being allowed more responsibilities and how the early struggles are past.

The difference to success is such a little amount of targeted help.

Happy I could help, happy the help took them this far. <3

Asked a new contractor representative on the preciseness of their hours on my project. The response was to volunteer to use Jira and log work and hours in detail., which is quite a time and energy investment. All I wanted was to discuss how the preciseness comes around, and check that the 50% allocation they've ended up with makes sense to them.

I have come to think of detailed hour reporting as a misplaced practice for inability to frame work otherwise.

We (the unidentified group) don't like the new direction #Playwright is taking with convenience functions and how the convenience function bloat makes their documentation less useful than it was before. The space of browser automation with all the tools is changing still quite heavily.

isn't one I immediately see as positive but it is what last year has seen.

Interesting is how much of the experience of many tools doing the work together, we have the habit of naming only one. Like we think we do "selenium" or "playwright" or "robot framework", even if there's a lot of ecosystem pieces that drive the experience we have. Libraries - or even frameworks - don't stand alone.

I have 10 newbies from LinkedIn who volunteered to explore this with me. I'm grateful for learning with them.

@raimohanska I use primarily playwright. There is a lot I like about it, and two main things that concern me: 1) real browsers are not its thing and the risk related to it is hard to grasp. 2) OSS but not community owned.

When #Selenium community gets out the BiDi work now ongoing, that is a big change. Creating SeleniumManager definitely helps a lot with browser management.

contentMap.en:
@raimohanska I use primarily playwright. There is a lot I like about it, and two main things that concern me: 1) real browsers are not its thing and the risk related to it is hard to grasp. 2) OSS but not community owned.

object.content: @raimohanska Also, the lines of *what is playwright* and *what is selenium* are fuzzier than ever. Playwright on JS is very different tool than Playwright on Python. Selenium is a lot closer to what playwright is on Python, while a lot of people in the community would recommend not using selenium but a framework that wraps selenium or uses the webdriver protocol. So we are often comparing things that aren't in the same exact space.

When you sketch a roadmap, you buffer in significant uncertainty yet ideas of sizes/shapes of things. When one size/shape abruptly changes, you should note and it pushes out something (or frees space). In the PO / team division of responsibilities, we often find ourselves making also the size/shape change something for the team to be responsible for, while teams really put their focus on the immediate work at hand.

Responsible by estimates. So much waste in premature estimation.

Programmers understand domains too. They care and think about customer problems and value too. There was a really fascinating dynamic on a discussion I needed to have around one line of code.

I had something that works and wanted to refactor to move it elsewhere.

My pair knew that what I had was not the best way that could be done.

I wanted to postpone best way and my pair did not.

So we split for some hours, I did what I wanted, they created sample of best way and eventually we merged.

We just could not find words to reconciliate the difference in the moment.

object.content:
A week ago I hijacked a teams test planning and did a plan that follows change. I reviewed the very small number of commits changing things from last accepted baseline, and created a table of my observations. I listed names of components changing, functional areas those components are part of and if with the change came unit tests.

My theory that I worked with in analysis is that changes in unit tests represent 1) tests failing and compulsory fixing or 2) dev thinking about testing the change.

object.content:
Especially if 2) is true, it lowers a particular type of risk.

Similarly, I know all of the devs and know which ones would never send out a change without trying it themselves, and which ones shortcut. So "who" changes things is part of the analysis.

The output document I created confused the next planner who got lost on a week of detailed unit test analysis.

Lesson learned: look at effort to produce an output. The process you imagine may be different from the one applied.

object.content:
So much of our design is push. It should be pull. Because when it is push, we do a few things that really don't help us.

We (over/under)estimate to block the push. Things pushed are things others have thought about for 5 months and we have just been shown, assuming the learning passes.

We redesign. Because we need to learn, and you learn when you actively think about it and there is no way of pushing someone else's model to us, we redo significant part of the work.

object.content:
Thinking of the three categories of friction for developer productivity: cognitive load, feedback loops and flow state.

Cognitive load is definitely growing with more people making changes in the area, and team size is making things harder.

Feedback loops are still slow and a bit random at arriving. Too often still we collect things of the week and things of the month together and struggle with the continuous.

Flow state is lack of interruptions and agency. Pull would help.

I am always fascinated with the math of time. In pairing today on 3 sessions, with longest session being 22 minutes the pair achieved something relevant. It was essentially the core of what today delivered. So it did not cost us 2 hours, but 2 days. And I am ok with that, just not the dishonesty of communication.

The unit of work is days or weeks. And it is rare (but exists) to change to smaller units of work for real.

object.content:
Three types of training:
1. Summaries. "Here's what the world seems to think about X"
2. War stories. "Here's me living through X"
3. Experiential. "Here's a simulation of X for your to try"

1 and 2 can be done with articles and books if people read, or with podcast and videos if they listen and watch. 3 requires classroom and every group is different.

I used to do a lot of 1&2 as training. Now I do a lot of 3.

Get past just reporting. One stretch at a time.

This pattern keeps repeating. One developer, two testers. Developer changes something, first tester tests the same thing developer already tested. Second tester does not trust (for good reasons) the first tester's idea of what testing should be done, and tests as well. And something really relevant is broken.

Being the second pair of eyes means you have to be able to add to the first pair. A whole lot of testers don't know how to do more than confirmatory testing.

object.content:
Calling property-based testing of an API "fuzzing" does not make it security testing.

Security testing is a form of functional testing where your tests are framed "negative". The functional testing approaches find security problems but analyzing the security problems for what their implications tend to be is slightly more complex than basic functional problems.

I am a little tired of people who specialize in security and do awareness.

We can control out reactions but not their choice of words. Our reactions drive a better future.

Some days I think I am unreasonable refusing the wrong silos.

I often talk about the results gap, which is like the invisible ink written list of unfinished work where #testing is the mechanism of making it visible.

Our gap became of uncontrollable size. I spent all yesterday visualising it with 35 items and estimating that the invisible list is currently about 150 things.

I annoys me that I let it get to this and that I feel like I should have done better. And I shouldn't have to be one doing this, which is also my failure.

object.content:
Been following cost of a pull request. We cut it by 17% from Q1 -> Q2 while ramping up lots of new team members. Now analyzing that we cut it 63% more from Q2 -> Q3 so far.

I work with the idea that nothing changes if we change nothing - for our customers, in our codebase including nowadays infra as code.

Obviously we know tons of ways of creating movement without value, but we knew it also when the costs per change were higher.

Two teams, the other has 7x cost per PR now.

Trying out a couple of tricks to frame #Selenium Open Space Conference.

We have enrolling with a PR (add yourself to page) to encourage frame of contributions. Will extend to issues as secondary route, since feedback is a contribution. Participating in conversations is a contribution.

We pre-announce session titles. Or rather, allow people to pre-announce them through PR to the page. People who have not been to open spaces fear no good content, and this is to mitigate that fear.

Doing things where you deliver a one hour session is never ‘just one hour’. Every task that interrupts your usual flow of focus puts a before and after pause. You’ll think about it. You’ll prepare. If successful, you’ll have conversations. Others will have conversations without you.

Questions, oh questions. Two favourites.

object.content:
Counted the test cases. 1699 tests in the sampled pipeline. A bit more of a breakdown:

Unit tests: 1187 (70%)
Component tests: 86 (5%)
Handcrafted system tests: 347 (20%)
Generated (MBT) system tests: 83 (5%)

61,8% code coverage with unit tests. All of this leaks bugs to be found in scale with attended testing approaches still but we'll get there.

With the conference conversation we broke the interoperability into its components.

First there was Alexa and Sonos, assistant with speaker and a speaker. Both have separate sound controls. Somehow normally turning Alexa sound down had generic impact, but Sonia could still have volume set to full.

In comes Spotify. It turns out that having connected it to this home system, allowed turning on music while binding it elsewhere. Now with full volume.

object.content: Last year, about this time we had been burned by consecutive failed recruitments to a team tester position. We got testers, but not the value of testers. I was accepted a weird intermediate, in effect loaned for 6 months at a time for each team to test and improve things from within, so I was not an option. We decided to not hire a tester and start sharing "tester hat" amongst developers. Everyone tests, but one tries to take extra time to help others notice what we may still be missing.

object.content:
Then my change of hearts happened. I decided to stop being the traveling tester in the organization and became manager of the team. Reluctant manager, but manager none the less. Manager of a team with no testers, but most definitely testing.

I became aware that in addition to the one team with no testers, we had two other teams. So I had three teams, two that had been mostly invisible to me before.

object.content:
That is how I got three testers.

I had a system specialist in need of a career and team change, that I needed to retrain to a programming-centric career path. So she changed teams and roles, and the team with two failed tester recruitments got a BRILLIANT tester, even while in training.

Two others were in a team of externals only, because their process says developers don't test. Also their process said testers don't design test cases, that is different role. Fixed the process.

object.content:
But fixing the process meant I removed one tester. So now we are at two. Where did the two others come from?

One came because I had the consultancy hiring power. It is not that I wanted a tester, I wanted a really good system test automation powerhouse and I knew one was just being let go from the previous product in our company. So I snatched the expert. Best thing ever. One more great team member, working across two teams.

The fourth came as I needed an agent of system in the third team.

A developer received a bug report on a thing that seemed like a tiny addition to a list of selections. A tester insist this should not be done as a late change, and if it is done, it should be tested a little further than just the change. After a bit of back and forth, the developer tests that the value added to the list get processed correctly in the next steps.

When testing, the developer discovers that the new value is not value like others, but it is a value over three fields.

What makes owning software more tolerable? It seems like a good question to ponder, given that I can easily say that finding new pieces you own in *yet another tech stack* after two years of working with the product really does not.

So I would go for saying having a reliable inventory would help. Assets that are executable (pipelines!) would help. Shared conventions of where things are would help. Architecture that allows rewriting pieces without rewriting the whole would help.

In a discussion with the brilliant Helena Jeret-Mäe on ensuring teaching becomes learned skills, I wrote down a personal realisation.

When I teach, I want us to be ok to fail in public. I want to teach we all fail, and we learn from both success and failure. Helena does really relevant work in learning space.

When a manager teaches their direct reports how to do the work better, it's not coaching or mentoring. It is teaching.

Also, feedback giving isn't coaching.

Reporting is easy. Fix isn’t.

object.content: Commercial companies and tracking are a different story than the same in all of open source. Free often means you sell your data (in a scale that grows) but it is a choice to go into that data business in the first place. With data comes the privacy and identifiable information, but also the rights to be forgotten and not tracked. I believe all tracking should be opt-in, and now I need to think about how much time that belief warrants from me.

After you've learned where you want to get and what might take you there, the difference of good results looks to boil down to two: bias to action (choose doing) and quality of collaboration (you won't get far alone).

object.content:
"Too much context switching"

When learning to drive a car, pedals, stick, wheel, looking around were all separate contexts. Years later the context is driving a car.

People who can barely test and think at same time call it context switching when they are asked to document in automation at same time. You are on the same task, it is not a switch. And you can go slow taking your time to rehearse the steps.

You're trying to go too fast for your level of skill. Internal locus of control.

2x return to sender for ‘I’ve tested this’. It is true they tested it. They spent time testing it. It’s just that the intent was off. Their intent was one of change regression testing when the risk they are investigating is the change is the wrong one.

They tested it changed. But the change is not the right change. And they would see it if they’d ask what the user does, not what the developer programmed.

Oh people of comms. Asking me how many (software) tests we run on average on a product during design phase.

First of all, there is no design phase for software. There is the phase of creating first truly use-worthy version, and in our context it takes years to get to that.

Second, while I count automation tests, large numbers may just show we are relying on wasting resources. I can easily go see we are running 600 000 tests annually for my product, but I think we're totally wasteful.

I listened to my 20-yo relative talk about how much they hate starting in a new job. As someone young and new, the first three months are about seeking balance on what subtasks each in pair / community do. They pointed out how with some work just flows and both carry their share. With some pairs, they do all and the other "manages" the young one. And with some they are sidelined as their work is not trusted.

We need to talk about how we share work.

@mlevison I have come to terms with the idea that while I want something, I am not entitled to require that from the other. I did not like it when I first learned that people lie from stages. Not just tell a single perspective, but completely fabricate stories.

I don't know why is this so hard, but I can say it is in practice. Six sources of "same but different" information.

1. Jira ticket (already closed 6 months ago) describes rules with limiting scope.
2. Confluence page describes rules without limiting scope AND has a comment changing the rules.
3. Confluence page tracks rules across three deployable subsystems.
4. Excel tracks what needs to be implemented in one of the subsystems.
5. Excel tracks what should be full scope across systems.

Four data points to "make a plan".
1) don't make a plan, just hack.
2) make a plan, tie to past experiences and focus on where experience is lacking on query
3) make a plan, focus on research, have theory but no practice in plan
4) start with why, and existing process, end with realism but with fear that shows struggle on not letting it stop you

Any of these could work, but I obviously have preferences.

I go to ConfEngine, with the idea of some exploratory testing to learn if this bug can be found with #Selenium and #Playwright tests. We do know that selenium automates browsers while playwright automates approximations of browsers, be it a superset of selected latest branded they have expanded to. Rathole!

But I have a video that shows it reproduces. So I analyze some more of that. I look at the exact browser version, and upgrade mine also to latest, no help. I look at the exact scenario, no help. I look at the addons, and I don't even know what all those are.

Following some of my ideas, I learn I find a way of reproducing a problem that looks like the one, and it is related to user rights. I have some the others don't. Could that be hiding the problem?

However, if that is the problem, then it's not browsers. I know the first reporter would be unlikely to not test on other browsers, and lo behold, the error messages just don't match on the dev tools. Same symptom, different causes. Rathole!

I write a talk proposal about browser testing and time. Resuming again.

The error message around cross origin request suggest it has to be settings difference or addon difference, and while it is browser, it's your browser not my browser.

object.content:
I get interrupted, and speak an hour with a really smart person about Conways law and why things I call architecture can just as well be organization design and we should collaborate to fix both.

And I still don't know how to set up a browser that would allow me to test if the bug can be found with both #Selenium and #Playwright. But I suspect that since it's really about the real browser, it can't.

Long story short, I am on vacation and I can fall into any ratholes I want to and I love it.

The agile-ish ideal of "just present the problem to the team and collaborate on the solution" relies on
1) ability to facilitate the conversation so that people's points for the conversation produce progress for the whole group
2) having people in the group that have skills and knowledge

Presenting a programming problem to a group of non-programmers probably isn't going to have a great solution.

object.content:
Thinking of trust and knowledge gap.

When what you know and what you need to know are different, there is a gap. But trust is what can cover some of the gap. You accept you don't know, you don't understand, and don't try to dig into the details.

I am struggling with experiences where people without product or architecture focus want to understand all of that to make decisions. They won't present the problem, but want to discuss solution details. And educating when gap is big is a lot.

Writing about intent over implementation. We are clearly struggling with this.

We said we want missing and incorrect data to show up as ///. Someone saw that this can happen, and closed up the ticket on it.

However, if I had data, and it becomes missing, that data is shown indefinitely. Because that is not missing data, that is time to live for existing data.

It can really be hard to have these conversations. Much harder than I would like.

Things people don't know graduating from IT relevant schools in Finland:

Difference between Docker Desktop - Docker Hub - Docker images in hosted artifactory.

Difference between Git - GitHub - hosted GitLab.

Feeling the love for the people who have taught me all this so that I can now wonder how new people know none of it.

object.content:
On conversation with Dr. Derek Cabrera on UpThinking, we're talking about practicing 5 moves of better thinking.
- zoom in
- zoom out
- take other's perspective
- recognize your bias
- see relationships

He is making a point that out of 10 people given a problem, 5 freeze. The 5 that don't freeze, apply moves. 25% do zoom in, 0% zoom out (enterprise thinking). 10% see relationships, <10 % takes other's perspective and 0% recognize their own bias.

#InternationalSystemsThinkingConf

When you have three options for running a tool you are asked to use, the order in which they are introduced may be meaningful:
- docker
- binaries
- source code

Starting with source code and building it locally makes your new tool use life unnecessarily complicated unless you already know you will need to have source to extend it.

This is not taught in schools.

object.content: For purposes of #ExploratoryTesting, I have been discussing the idea that the software you are testing is your external imagination. object.content: I used to work with security software with risks exactly like this - possibility of taking down millions of Windows machines. This whole incident reminds me we too, decade(s) ago had problem like this that test coverage missed. But we had a few other mechanisms that protected us:

contentMap.en: I used to work with security software with risks exactly like this - possibility of taking down millions of Windows machines. This whole incident reminds me we too, decade(s) ago had problem like this that test coverage missed. But we had a few other mechanisms that protected us:

object.content:
1) Delay-based distribution: the group who would get things first was small but reactive, and rendering a board member's computer useless without manual intervention did a lot of good for investments in ensuring the lessons were learned without impacting customers
2) Eating own dogfood in company: we learned to distribute internally continuously, and segment distributions. The whole environment for testing was built to provide HUMAN interventions because test systems fail.

contentMap.en:
1) Delay-based distribution: the group who would get things first was small but reactive, and rendering a board member's computer useless without manual intervention did a lot of good for investments in ensuring the lessons were learned without impacting customers
2) Eating own dogfood in company: we learned to distribute internally continuously, and segment distributions. The whole environment for testing was built to provide HUMAN interventions because test systems fail.

object.content:
3) Throttling, autorevert, secondary update channels: we built a number of features that would enable us to fix things without showing up face to face
4) Architectural rewrites: isolating risks like this, because not all software causes blue screens.

contentMap.en:
3) Throttling, autorevert, secondary update channels: we built a number of features that would enable us to fix things without showing up face to face
4) Architectural rewrites: isolating risks like this, because not all software causes blue screens.

object.content: And then there was the continuous investment on test coverage. I am disappointed if the conclusion is that test coverage is what they missed, when they have a wealth of investments their board members would happily sponsor to never see this happen to them again.

I did the legwork to allow for use of GitHub copilot on production code a year ago for a particular product. The legwork included risk assessments, upgrades of tool versions and compensations.

Compensations were three fold:
1) we would be allowed to say in public in more detail that usual the experiences we had
2) we would use time on open source projects
3) we would donate money to sustaining open source

While code-generation tools in AI space may be legal, they are not ethical.

I’ve been tasked with assessment projects with four types of framing now.

1) productivity. This software development and maintenance is expensive, can we do something about it.

2) pipelines. We want more things captured in code, what next.

3) skills. We got testers are they any good? Is there a missing testing capability or practice. What they need to learn?

4) process and ways of working / benchmarking. How the agreements and problems map to those I’ve seen elsewhere.

object.content:
Thinking about skills. Some skills we're assessed on are "painting with blue color" skills. They are specific experiences, like if you tested on AWS or Azure, and people don't consider you right if you don't show you have painted with blue color before.

However, painting with enough colors, they are all colors, and you acquire "painting with rainbow" skills. This raises the abstraction, and enables you to do things well beyond the individual colors. You even find shades in your blue.

Three reasons why I would consider this low code thing in this acceptance testing.

1. The business processes they test, they also do in production manually. There's a reuse possibility between acceptance testing and robotic process automation.

2. They don't want to push the copy of production environment down to teams for reasons, and some of the testing really can't happen anywhere else than with acceptance testing.

3. They want to limit the options. All tools do the job they have.

I prefer applying the modern tools if we already have ideas left and down in place.

4=>IV often
4=>IIII in luxury watches and old clock towers

Just like with falsehoods programmers believe about time, I expect testers to be aware of this.

I seem to be repeating myself again.

Applying AI in testing to do test practices that are already wasteful to do wasteful things faster is not my goal.

For a lot of issues in testing, we have good answers that are not AI. If you don't know your coverage, observability in your application can help with that more. If 50% of your tests fail, isolating ones that pass and fixing flakiness on the rest does not need to be AI.

The "we must use AI to be more productive" conversation yesterday lead to concluding:

Anecdotally, we used GitHub Copilot, it did not have impact on our pull request output flow metric where we worked from idea that nothing change if you change nothing.

During same timeframe, we experimented with moving from blocking code reviews to ship-show-ask which had 4x productivity impact.

There's plenty we could do for productivity, starting with limiting WIP that could be non-AI.

When development teams state to their customers they can't assess performance because customer did not set performance requirements, what are they really saying? I am thinking back to a tester way back who refused to test without "requirement". A developer gave them one, said <0.01 seconds response times. The real need was to express *how long is that now* and *what are consequences of it*.

object.content:
Having conversations about copyrights and licenses makes me realize it might be good we talk about this stuff a bit.

Having material you created available in the public does not mean you can take it and use it. If license is not visible, it's the most limited one you should assume, not the most permissible one.

The copyright owner gets to set the license. I have to decades of licensing my materials as CC-BY and I am now making next generations that are licensed CC-BY-NC-SA.

Within Robot Framework ecosystem, there are (at least) three libraries for driving browsers:
- qweb library
- selenium library
- browser library

I have been asking people in various conversations to compare and contrast the three. If they are aware (usually not), they have no idea what the differences are.

Saying you have RF expertise and all you know is keywords from one library using the html doc reference, feels a little light to me.

object.content:
Two repeated patterns on how test automation fails.
1) gym membership. Orgs fall into marketing promise of commercial tool and licenses end up on the shelf. Use beyond proof of concept does not happen.
2) island of one. Orgs choose an open source test tool that has simplified language that developers in teams don't touch. After two or more rounds of restarts, they realize the tool needs to be chosen for team, not the individual.

Looking at tester:developer ratios. I have a collection of projects where the ratio is none:some. The drivers to having no testers seem to be:
- Developers test. Can test. Want to test.
- Testers without domain expertise add handoffs but not enough value.
- Testers with domain expertise aren't testers but business folks in the customer organizations. And cheaper to use as tester by direct cost while not necessarily by opportunity cost.

object.content:
Stop calling it "integration testing" when it is
1) end to end testing with everything but user interface
2) subsystem testing of two interconnected systems
3) data filtering / rules testing over a set of APIs, or a single API

It is one of the least meaningful choices of words you can choose to describe functional testing focused on parts that may not be available without deployment.

attachment.name:
Value Statements Capturing Ideas that Drive Us

No product owner - product owned by team, with shared ownership
Nothing changes if we change nothing - bias to moving forward to better over extensive planning
On-time planning - plan details just before plan is executed, but plan for themes continuously
Collaborating with others over individual productivity
Documentation as output - writing documentation at time we know the most, as things we leave behind for our future selves
Socialize over documenting for process - share way of working by working this way together, including all team members; follow behaviors expected over following rules.
Value over compliance. There is always reasons on why we have compliance rules in place. Go back to discussing the value we seek a compliance activity to create.
Proposed requirements become requirements at time of 1st release of them. They are a result of negotiation under constraints of design.

1. automation (with contemporary exploratory testing twist). Automation is non-negotiable skill. But so is testing.
2. ERP/CRM platform testing, with automation. Less automation but still automation. Usually low code tools.
3. Leading testing remotely. Ownership here in Finland, teams distributed globally.

Specialized skill asked is performance testing.

I know its hard to grasp but:

- the software you are using can reach end of life because the organization that created chooses so

- the path forward may not be a simple upgrade to version, because hardware + OS requirements evolve too

- purchasing "maintenance" does not include all maintenance, esp. in cases like EOL

Software that does not change is dead. While it's used, it changes.

object.content:
I am choosing what to recommend in test automation. I have 5 options:
1. Use what they use already (usually a small tool vendor)
2. Use LeapWork
3. Use UIPath
4. Use Robot Framework
5. Use Open Source with real programming language

I am heavily inclined towards 5. I know the availability of people is high in 4&5, medium in 3 and low in 1&2. 1&2&3 come with significant money out of pocket and promises rarely realized, of "citizen developers".

I don't think selecting is the key to success.

You wrote some code, enough to create a component. You packaged that component, and you attached a license to it. The component and its source is now subject to that license.

If it's MIT, that allows use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and sell copies. So taking a piece of that code, attribution remains.

Ideas aren't protected. Inspiration is not protected. Looking at how someone did something and doing it similar / better is not protected.

This seems like nice illustration why testing is about filtering problems on unit, integration and system levels, as separate perspectives.

A guy get emails advertising the same service (doctor).

1. Birthday discount
2. Common ad
3. Best available [MISSING]

Costs are 3 > 2 > 1. The ad he should get from filtering problems is 3 (system). You'd notice 1 should never be sent comparing to 1 (integration). He got all since they were assessed only on unit level.

object.content:
In this era of productivity talk, is software development actually becoming more expensive?

We discussed a few anecdotes:

A project where the cost of work now is the same but the cost of cloud doubles the costs on a monthly basis, and the sense of value is the same.

Two projects where discussions about testing did not change quality/outcome as such but gave a factor to multiply the costs.

Have we been layering things we could drop?

Responsibility. That of an organization and that of an individual. And what if things go wrong, who is liable?

The liability theme has been big on my decisions on future hobbies, and I am not keen on being liable to pitch in uncontrollable effort to governance to not be negligent in position of responsibility.

What I learned though is that in public organizations, this takes extreme measures with stories of being convicted and paid compensation as employee of an org.

The world we live in. The risk being "responsible" can hold for directors. Quite a system.

I was 17 and my friend started believing everyone was against her except our closely knit group of friends. She told me a guy from our class was harassing her. I confronted the guy and talked to him about correcting his behavior. While he looked confused, he took it fine.

A year later my friend was diagnosed.

Even when we’re healthy, we frame experiences with our internal dialog. And I can’t tell the difference when people around me are no longer healthy.

A small infographic that is mostly text on picture about regression testing, describing there are five flavors of it.

Representative environment: We run these automated tests daily, but when we run them on *this* environment, they're regression tests. 

Unintended side effects: We look for anything that worked but no longer does, mostly without intending to break it.

Embarrassment protection: We don't understand side effects so let's schedule time to make sure nothing visible in main flows breaks.

Bugs return: We don't have reliable version control and fixes we make vanish, and we just said they were fixed... 

Granular feedback of past intent: Automation designed fast to run isolates each change to note side effects.

A year ago joining here, I came to a pocket of Robot Framework. Since we, like so many other consultancies, source companies with Robot Framework programmers (they call them testers), most of my work is to support growth and survival within that ecosystem.

However, my head and experiences say a change is on its way. A change of general purpose programming language for testing as bridge with other developers.

object.content: In first three months, I discovered a pattern in customers. Developers took over test automation on side of other programming.

It may sound to you like you are given a task, but as part of intake, think about the unique value you enrich to the task as you do it.

Doing what you are told is not unique enrichment.

Doing what is needed, and doing it exceptionally well is a much better framing.

And no matter what you do, don't send them an AI generated piece without your forewords. Don't leave them correcting AI when you were in the loop already.

Coaching exploratory testing as a senior exploratory tester. Notes to self.

- No matter how they prioritize, they better have a story. That is a story of how valuable the information is, more than how much of that information there is.

- Have better model of what could be different if you test in two environments. Understand how data and function are separate while intertwined.

- Tell me what has not been done. I care for you recognizing work remaining more than work done.

Year one, I made myself available. I broadcast information as samples to what I could help with. Only a few people took initiative of connecting.

Year two, I made changes. More hands-on again. More ensemble and pair work. A little less saying and a little more showing. And the culture started to change.

It might be sticking with the problems longer. Or it might be the approach change. Regardless, staying around and observing if probes impact behaviors is necessary.

Silly little drawings time again, for automation framing. I did a lot of work on dropping the ideas of "exploratory testing is manual" and "test automation", making programmatic tests something that you run as attended or unattended. Bets having to say that you have "manual test automation", which is the most popular form of automation I help organizations move from.

So today it was the other dimension of waste in models. Programmatic tests are worth more if you don't frame the as regression.

We agreed when to meet, but no (virtual) location. Should I send the invite, as I am recruiting? But I am recruiting someone who does not treat me as their assistant, and they could show me they understand my pain by just volunteering.

So I am thinking: if I don't move, we don't meet. Which one of us - or both - lose out on the deadlock?

Why always me?

Did my 1st "Yes, we will sponsor a conference" decision, and lived to regret it.

First of all, paying out money from a corporation is far from straightforward. The work of being pinged around to not end up with knowledge on how this is done is outstanding. Those who know, know. I don't.

I have, implicitly, placed the bar to products that are used not just built.

I started the classification to make a point of having already a lot of value in becoming better at using. But using does not create IPR.

On today's news, the piece on Accenture's plans on letting go people who have not learned to use AI.

- do companies really think throwing videos at people is training their employees

I have been playing with the lifelong learning vs. taskwide learning, and how learning is not expected to be chunked smaller and over longer timeframe.

object.content:
When we inherit maintenance of a buggy system that is ‘good enough quality’, the missing we test against is not higher quality but ‘avoid making it worse or bad in new ways’. That mission is a solid starting point for contemporary exploratory testing.

Explaining to a colleague how exploratory testing does not mean going on finding and fixing everything. Information that matters varies.

QA is not testing. It's more like the rules we all play by.

And telling me it is because RF has three files and cucumber has one is just poppycock.

Talked to a client test lead yesterday. The only one they have, in a company where we used to have 10.

‘Testing has a reputation problem’, she said. ‘It still is getting cut out when recognized by titles or by phases’. ‘I call it quality assurance and it lives longer’.

The conversation continued with a realization: her own experiences of contractor testing lead her believe it didn’t work. ‘Only business users know enough to do a good job testing.’

object.content:
The "you can take the call", and decision-avoidance.

One of the first things I remember learning on exploratory testing is the idea that there are options, and you are making the choices. They aren't given to you with magic power of method, but you are supposed to be in control of having options.

I presented two options today, and "you can take the call". When in fact I want us to start tracking that taking the call is equally divided, but also founded on versatile options.

Due to budget cuts, a tester was moved from 100% to 50% allocation. I kept asking if we cut the work and the value, or only the work. So we analyzed metrics.

We cut the work, and doubled the value.

We still would process 40 changes a month and test them. We would plan based on risks better. And since the work includes less learning of the system on later years, learning got cut from the hours almost completely.

Finding problems outside *this change* was down. But contributing specs was up.

One of those "difference of a task and a budget" conversations. If you are told you can use three weeks, that is budget. If you are told you should write test plan, that is task.

The task may take you two days, and you can't just use the budget if you can't make a sensible case of making your plan more.

Plenty of ways for "more". But waiting is not one of those things.

These aren't yes and no responses.

AI, for me is *external imagination* and *task expansion*. Trust is less relevant than harm.

This public procurement is blowing my mind. First the client defines what problem they have that they are procuring for. Then they describe the problem in terms of requirements. And often miss many things. This way they get a price with a vendor, and choose with criteria of price and "quality", meaning whatever requirements they cooked up.

Let's say they bought it for 100. Anything unclear in their requirements changes it from 100 to 1000, no new bid completion. Underestimating to win it is.

In preparing a joined talk on lessons learned on experiential learning of AI in testing, my pair's lessons all gravitate to one thing: uncertainty.

The world she moves into this is one where testing was requirements, and there was certainty on when you were done. Architecture was someone else's responsibility. Your work was constrained and certain.

AI forced her into the developer's uncertainty in generating code, and I made it worse by introducing exploratory testing eradicating certainty.

object.content:
Just like everyone else, I created an agent that looks at a pull request and scopes test automation selection to what was changed to save time. Not complicated.

But is that valuable? Not convinced. Saves up time in running end to end, but so would random selection. Randomness would not fake that the selection if grounded and thought through.

I would claim this is such a waste. And not running all your tests is excuse to accept flaky.

If you've been promised "unit testing" contractually, it does not automatically mean you get the repeated 80% code coverage after each change. Or have invested in having that.

object.content:
Demoed exploratory testing with agents, and now processing the comments. Essentially people don't like the fact that I have collapsed roles together and reordered tasks taxonomy for better results faster.

At least I become more aware of how differently I test:

- I go directly to feedback from the application, and map back to tracking-requirements without going through test cases

object.content:
Looks like there is (at least) three layers of testing for this AI upgrade of 1M lines of Java code, and new team-level vocabulary to talk about it.

The *generator tests* are systematically generated with AI on a recipe that includes example tests driven by code coverage and property based testing.

The *behavior tests* are existing test base. They risk needing to change in ways that we can't quite control, but they hold our past truth.

The *prod playback tests* are our new approach on the risks of change we can't even pinpoint.

And we need to add *future maintenance assessment* because we'll live with what we leave behind.

object.content:
The disconnect of calendar time and working days is what fascinates me today.

Same work of running a genAI thing is 10h invoiced from one, 120 hours from another. The same work is 2 weeks calendar time from one, 4 weeks calendar time from another.

There is, clearly, a bit of learning for 2 that 1 has already acquired. But the most significant factor is that 1 does not *need* to log hours here if they can attend elsewhere and log hours there. 2 has no other place to log hours that is acceptable.

And then someone runs conclusion based on hour data. Oh dear.

When pairing on *Catch the Bugs* application today, we had a list of features to add from, and yet we added something else. The something else was more important, but we had not added it to the list.

Reflecting what happened we discussed that both in the pair are people who find it easier to generate new ideas and follow the energy, than follow through on a plan and stay on track. The tendency works well with exploring. Both in the pair are quite capable with mechanisms of staying on track, even if those aren't the first instinct.

This way around, we can choose to reprioritize. Without seeing new options, there is no choice but the plan. Not seeing options is my day-to-day frustration.

object.content:
When you talk to enough people with granularity, you start modeling the similarities and differences. This time on splitting the "have you used AI" to 27 distinct experience classes that lead you a little further than 1) I asked it a question and 2) I gave it everything to summarize.

My team of testing, 81% SOMEONE experience coverage and 37% of EVERYONE experience coverage. And I have been teaching through these experiences for a year now.

object.content:
When I complained about meetup making waiting list a paid functionality, a fellow tester decided a good course of action was to publicly tell me I could close the dialog from the x in the corner.

I was awfully blunt pointing out that if that works, it’s one of those works on someone else’s machine or in older memories.

Comments: deleted. I know getting corrected in public is uncomfortable but I find the need of silently editing history fascinating.

object.content:
1,71 €. Reality of token cost for a particular task. When people expected thousands and got this, what is the gap?

I am modeling the gap. There are positive reasons to it (reuse, targeted scope) and negative reasons to it (scope expectations, delayed risk to learn). Using a cheap slot machine is great if it does the work. Using an expensive slot machine the same. Appearance of work is prevalent.

object.content:
Refused to submit a proposal to a conference, insisting that I let them know that if they would want something I can contribute, I have now told them I am available. Asking for free work beyond that is not right, and is not for me at this time.

They submitted my two ideas from the conversation we had themselves.

Conferences should do their own work of sourcing great content and not rely on people who can afford to copy paste proposals in their submission systems.

object.content:
I interviewed a knowledge worker (sales) about their use of AI at work. One of the experiences I was tracking was if they have pitched a solution with AI.

I did not expect the response. They have, but every single one of them has turned into the client taking the idea and running with it.

The ideas have a different position now.
